title: DID GOD APPROVE OF CONCUBINES?
paragraphs: DID GOD APPROVE OF CONCUBINES?
The Bible Records Men Having Them. But Does That Mean God Wanted Them?
There is a question hiding inside some of the Bible’s most uncomfortable stories.
Abraham had Hagar.
Jacob had Bilhah and Zilpah.
David had concubines.
Solomon had hundreds.
And because the Bible does not erase these men from its pages—because some of them were even used mightily by God—an unsettling question eventually rises:
Did God actually approve of concubines?
Be careful with the answer.
Because if we read the Bible as though everything it records is something it recommends, we can make Scripture endorse almost anything.
The Bible records murder.
It records incest.
It records adultery.
It records drunkenness, betrayal, polygamy, rape, slavery, idolatry, political corruption, family dysfunction, and horrifying violence.
But recording something truthfully is not the same thing as approving it morally.
Sometimes Scripture tells you, “Thus says the LORD.”
Sometimes Scripture tells you, in effect, “This is what fallen human beings did.”
And knowing the difference changes everything.
The Hebrew word commonly translated “concubine” is פִּילֶגֶשׁ — pilegesh.

It refers to a woman in a recognized relationship with a man that possessed marital or quasi-marital characteristics but generally did not carry the same social standing as a primary wife. The exact legal and social circumstances varied across the ancient world and across individual biblical narratives, so we should resist forcing every concubine mentioned in Scripture into one modern category.
But one thing becomes painfully clear as the biblical story unfolds:
God did not introduce concubinage in Eden.
Human beings did.
Go back before Abraham.
Before Jacob.
Before David.
Before Solomon.
Before Israel had kings, armies, palaces, or dynasties.
Go back to the beginning.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew speaks of אִישׁ — ish, “man,” and אִשָּׁה — ishshah, “woman/wife,” moving into the covenantal reality Scripture describes as בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad:
“one flesh.”
That is the picture at creation.
Not one man accumulating women according to wealth, power, fertility, politics, or desire.
One-flesh covenant.
And centuries later, when Jesus was questioned about marriage, He did something extraordinarily important.
He went back to creation.
Jesus said:

“Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female… Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh?”
Then He declared:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Matthew 19:4–6.
The Greek expression is οἱ δύο — hoi duo:
“the two.”
Jesus did not point His hearers toward the complicated households of Abraham, Jacob, David, or Solomon as the definition of marriage.
He pointed them backward.
To Eden.
To God’s intention before sin had twisted human relationships.
And that distinction matters enormously.
Because someone can ask, “But didn’t God allow these arrangements?”
Yes—in the sense that Scripture describes a fallen world in which practices existed that God regulated without thereby establishing them as His original ideal.
Regulation is not necessarily endorsement.
Jesus Himself gives us the principle.
Speaking about divorce, He said Moses permitted divorce “because of your hardness of heart,” but then added:
“from the beginning it was not so.”
Matthew 19:8.
Read that again.
“From the beginning it was not so.”
There are things God addressed within fallen human societies because sinful people were already doing them.
That does not mean those things represented Eden.
That does not mean brokenness became holiness merely because God placed boundaries around human behavior.
And suddenly the stories of concubinage begin looking very different.
Consider Abraham.
God promised Abraham descendants.
But the promise seemed impossible.
Sarah was barren.
Years passed.
Bodies aged.
Hope became painful.
And Genesis 16 records Sarah giving Hagar, her Egyptian servant, to Abraham in an attempt to obtain children through her.
Genesis does not present this as a glorious demonstration of faith.
The household fractures almost immediately.
Hagar conceives.
Tension erupts.
Sarah becomes bitter.
Hagar suffers.
Hagar flees.
A child is eventually born into a conflict he did not create.
And yet here is where the Gospel-shaped beauty of Scripture begins appearing even in the wreckage.
God sees Hagar.
The woman caught inside somebody else’s desperate attempt to control the promise discovers that heaven has not forgotten her.
She calls the LORD:
אֵל רֳאִי — El Roi.
“The God who sees me.”
Genesis 16:13.
That should stop us.
Because Scripture is not merely telling the stories of powerful patriarchs.
God sees the wounded people standing in the shadows of their decisions too.
Maybe that is why this subject matters more than we think.
Concubinage is not merely an ancient theological puzzle.
It exposes something painfully modern.
Human beings still try to rewrite God’s boundaries whenever obedience becomes inconvenient.
We still rename compromise.
We still justify what benefits us.
We still point toward somebody else’s failure and say, “See? They did it.”
We still confuse God’s patience with God’s approval.
We still want biblical characters to give us permission for things the biblical story itself is warning us about.
Jacob’s household becomes another painful example.
Through Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, and Zilpah, Jacob fathers the sons who become the foundation of Israel’s tribes.
And yes, God sovereignly works through that family.
But sovereignty is not endorsement.
God accomplishing His purpose through human dysfunction does not make the dysfunction righteous.
Look at the household.
Jealousy.
Competition.
Women desperately fighting for affection.
Children becoming entangled in rivalry.
Brothers eventually selling Joseph into slavery.
The family through whom God would bring covenant blessing is simultaneously a family desperately in need of grace.
That is one of Scripture’s recurring messages:
God can accomplish holy purposes through deeply broken people without calling their brokenness holy.
Then comes David.
The man after God’s own heart.
The psalmist.
The warrior.
The king.
And a man whose sexual and family failures eventually brought catastrophic pain into his household.
Deuteronomy had already warned Israel’s future king:
“He shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.”
Deuteronomy 17:17.
That command existed before David occupied Jerusalem.
And long before Solomon filled his palace.
So when Scripture later tells us that David acquired additional wives and concubines, the mere fact that the historical narrative records it cannot erase the standard God had already revealed.
Some readers raise 2 Samuel 12:8, where through Nathan God describes giving David Saul’s house and Saul’s wives “into your arms” or “into your bosom.”
Does that prove God morally commanded David to practice polygamy or concubinage?
That conclusion goes beyond what the passage requires.

The context is Nathan confronting David after David committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged Uriah’s death. The language emphasizes everything associated with Saul’s royal house and kingdom being placed under David’s authority. It magnifies the enormity of David’s ingratitude: God had given him abundance, yet David seized what belonged to another man.
Whatever complexities surround the ancient royal-household language, 2 Samuel 12 cannot reasonably be used to cancel Deuteronomy 17:17 or the creation pattern to which Jesus Himself later appeals.
And then there is Solomon.
If sheer biblical description meant divine approval, Solomon would be the strongest case imaginable.
First Kings 11:3 tells us:
“He had 700 wives, who were princesses, and 300 concubines.”
A thousand women.
Power beyond imagination.
Political alliances.
Royal prestige.
Everything an ancient king could use to convince himself that excess meant blessing.
Then Scripture gives the verdict.
“His wives turned away his heart.”
1 Kings 11:3.
There it is.
The very danger Deuteronomy warned about became Solomon’s tragedy.
The wisest king alive became foolish enough to allow divided affection to produce divided worship.
The issue was not simply that Solomon had “too much love.”
His heart moved away from exclusive loyalty to the LORD.
That is where sin eventually takes us.
It promises expansion.
Then produces fragmentation.
It promises freedom.
Then demands allegiance.
It tells us God will understand.
Then slowly teaches our hearts to live without asking what God actually desires.
And perhaps nowhere is the ugliness surrounding concubinage more emotionally devastating than Judges 19.
There, a concubine becomes the victim of horrific sexual violence and dies.
The chapter is supposed to disturb you.
Judges is showing a society collapsing under sin.
Its recurring diagnosis is chilling:
“Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.”
Judges 21:25.
That is not a celebration of Israelite morality.
It is an indictment of it.
The Bible refuses to airbrush what human rebellion does to people.
Especially vulnerable people.
Especially women.
Especially those whose suffering powerful people would rather forget.
That is one reason the Bible can be so uncomfortable.
It tells the truth.
It does not manufacture flawless heroes.
Abraham needs grace.
Jacob needs grace.
Judah needs grace.
David needs grace.
Solomon needs grace.
You need grace.
I need grace.
And perhaps this is where the question changes.
We began by asking:
“Did God approve of concubines?”
But underneath that question may be another one.
“What has God tolerated in my life that I have mistaken for His approval?”
That question gets closer.
Maybe nothing catastrophic happened after your compromise.
Maybe the relationship survived.
Maybe nobody discovered the messages.
Maybe the addiction remains hidden.
Maybe the bitterness has become so familiar that you call it personality.
Maybe you keep saying, “God understands,” when deep inside you know the Holy Spirit has been calling you to surrender.
God’s patience should never be confused with permission.
Romans 2:4 says that God’s kindness is meant to lead us to repentance.
Not deeper into hiding.
Repentance.
The Greek word is μετάνοια — metanoia.
It carries the idea of a changed mind, a turning—a transformation of how we understand our sin before God that produces a changed direction.
Christian repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Judas felt terrible.
Repentance turns toward God.
It brings the hidden thing into the light.
It stops negotiating.
It stops asking how close to the edge we can live while still calling ourselves faithful.
And this is where Jesus becomes more than the conclusion to an argument about ancient marriage.
Jesus becomes our only hope.
Because if the Bible were merely a record of good people earning God’s approval, its pages would be remarkably empty.
Instead, Scripture is filled with scandal.
Broken families.
Sexual failure.
Deception.
Violence.
Pride.
Betrayal.
People making promises they cannot keep.
People receiving mercy they do not deserve.
And through all that wreckage, God keeps moving history toward Christ.
Jesus does not enter the story because humanity finally became respectable.
He enters because humanity needs redemption.
At the cross, Jesus does not call evil good.
He bears sin’s judgment.
He does not redefine rebellion until it becomes acceptable.
He offers forgiveness to rebels.
He does not tell sinners to clean themselves perfectly before approaching Him.
He calls them to repent and believe.
And the blood of Christ reaches places shame told you God would never touch.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain unchanged.
Power to become new.
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.”
2 Corinthians 5:21.
Christianity is not the announcement that your past never mattered.
It is the announcement that your past does not have to be your master anymore.
Maybe your scandal does not involve concubines.
Maybe it was adultery.
Pornography.
A secret relationship.
A divorce filled with wounds nobody understands.
Sex outside marriage.
A pregnancy surrounded by shame.
Years of manipulation.
A marriage you damaged.
Someone you betrayed.
Someone who betrayed you.
Or maybe your scandal has nothing to do with sexuality at all.
Maybe it is pride.
Greed.
Hatred.
Religious hypocrisy.
A hidden addiction.
A double life.
You know the sentence you are terrified someone will someday say about you.
Jesus already knows it.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
Repent.
Come home.
Receive mercy.
Follow Christ.
Let Him change you.
This is why the Bible’s broken characters should never become excuses for our sin.
They should become evidence that God is astonishingly capable of redeeming sinners.
The scandal is real.
But grace gets the final word for everyone who comes to Christ.
You do not have to publish the details of your private struggle. Simply comment, “No more hiding,” if today you are choosing surrender over excuses.
Or comment, “Jesus, forgive me,” if your heart knows exactly what needs to be brought before Him.
And if you are exhausted from fighting, comment, “Pray for me.”
There are moments when another believer needs to know that the person sitting silently beside them is fighting too.
Not because saving a post makes anyone righteous, but because there may come a night when compromise starts sounding reasonable again and you need to remember:
God’s patience is not permission.
His grace is calling you home.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in worship, obedience, love, generosity, truth, and lives surrendered to Him.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of helping biblical truth reach another person.
Jesus is calling sinners home.
The God who saw Hagar still sees the forgotten.
The God who disciplined David still forgives the repentant.
The God who warned Solomon still calls divided hearts back to Himself.
And the Savior who spoke about marriage by pointing humanity back to the beginning is also the Savior who went to a cross to redeem people who have wandered far from God’s design.
So do not use Abraham to excuse what God is asking you to surrender.
Do not use David to baptize compromise.
Do not use Solomon to make excess look harmless.
Do not mistake what Scripture records for what God recommends.
Look instead at Jesus.
Look at the cross.
Look at the empty tomb.
There is your standard.
There is your mercy.
There is your hope.
There is your way home.
Someone needs your testimony.
Someone needs to discover that repentance did not destroy you.
It brought you home.
Someone needs to hear that grace did not make your sin acceptable.
Grace made redemption possible.
Because perhaps the most shocking thing in all these scandalous biblical stories is not that human beings could fall so terribly.
We already know they can.
The shocking thing is that God kept pursuing sinners.
Until eventually He came Himself.
And when the nails went through the hands of Jesus, God proved once and for all that He was not interested in pretending our scandal did not exist.
He intended to redeem us from it.
Never confuse God’s patience with His approval—but never confuse the depth of your failure with the limit of His grace.
